O Futur II, passo a passo: The Futur II, step by step
PASSO 1: o FUTUR II usa «WERDEN» (conjug: STEP 1: the FUTUR II uses «WERDEN» (conjugated) + PARTIZIP II + «HABEN» or «SEIN» (infinitive, at the end): «Er wird das Buch gelesen haben», «Er wird angekommen sein.» This is English "will have read", "will have arrived" — but German sends «haben/sein» to the very end. STEP 2: USE 1: something that will be COMPLETED at a point in the future: «Bis morgen werde ich es geschafft haben» (by tomorrow I will have managed it). STEP 3: USE 2: an ASSUMPTION about the PAST, with «wohl», «wahrscheinlich», «vermutlich»: «Er wird wohl krank gewesen sein» (he must have been ill). English uses "must have" here, not "will have". STEP 4: the choice between «haben» and «sein» is the one from the Perfekt (movement and change of state → «sein»). STEP 5: in practice, the Futur II is rare in speech; assumptions are its most common use. STEP 6: compare: Futur I («Er wird kommen»: he will come) × Futur II («Er wird gekommen sein»: he will have come, or he must have come).
o português tem o futuro do pretérito co: English has «will have done» for something completed in the future and «must have done» for an assumption about the past. German covers both with the Futur II: werden + Partizip II + haben/sein.
Suposição sobre o passado: werden + Part: Assumption about the past: werden + Partizip II + sein.

PASSO 1: as PARTÍCULAS MODAIS são palavr: STEP 1: MODAL PARTICLES are short little words with NO fixed translation: they give the sentence a TONE (friendly, insistent, surprised). They sit in the middle of the sentence, after the verb and the subject — never at the start. STEP 2: «DOCH» strengthens an invitation or something obvious: «Komm doch mit!» (come on, come along!), «Das ist doch klar!» (but that's obvious!). STEP 3: «MAL» softens a request, like English "just": «Komm mal her!» (come here a sec). STEP 4: «JA» reminds the other person of something they already know: «Du hast ja gestern gearbeitet» (you worked yesterday, remember?). It does NOT mean "yes" here. STEP 5: «EBEN» and «HALT» (more colloquial) show that's just how it is: «Das ist eben so», «Das ist halt so.» STEP 6: the choice depends on the tone: use them to sound natural, but do not translate them word for word.

«mal» fica antes do prefixo/complemento: «mal» goes before the separable prefix / complement at the end.

PASSO 1: «DENN» suaviza uma pergunta: «W: STEP 1: «DENN» softens a question: «Wie geht es dir denn?» (so how are you?). It is NOT "because" here. STEP 2: «EIGENTLICH» means "actually": «Was machst du eigentlich?» STEP 3: «WOHL» expresses an assumption: «Er ist wohl krank» (he's probably ill). STEP 4: «SCHON» reassures: «Das wird schon klappen» (it'll work out, don't worry). It is NOT "already" here. STEP 5: «ABER» marks surprise: «Das ist aber nett!» (how kind!). It is NOT "but" here. STEP 6: «RUHIG» gives relaxed permission: «Du kannst ruhig früher gehen» (feel free to leave early). STEP 7: «VIELLEICHT» in an exclamation: «Das war vielleicht ein Tag!» (what a day that was!). STEP 8: use particles in speech, not in formal writing.
